name: Jamal Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a grader at the Saltpan Ridge lithium mine. My job is the haul roads: I keep them smooth and cambered so the big trucks don't shake themselves apart or slide off when it rains. It sounds boring, but a good road saves the company a fortune in tyres, and the truck drivers wave when you've done it right. The worst part is the dust in the dry months, it gets into everything, my lunch, my ears, my marriage.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My wife Nadia jokes that she married a man and got a bag of dust. She runs a little café on Main Street called the Pick and Kettle, mostly miners getting breakfast before shift. We put almost everything we had into the coffee machine and the fit-out two years ago, so we've got less than a month of money in the bank. The plan is the café becomes our retirement when I stop at about sixty-three. Our three kids are grown and scattered, one's a teacher, two are in the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, it's a tool like any other. I use it a bit for the café, working out prices and writing the specials board. At work I'd say the same: some people got worked up for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me fine. Lithium's growing, the mine's hiring, and the café lives off the miners. If nothing much changes, our plan works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep grading roads and keep helping Nadia on my days off. Maybe use the AI a bit more for the café's books, since it's saving her an hour a week already. We'd try to get a month's savings back over the next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Comfortable, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the café lives off the miners. How many come in on a normal day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a weekday, maybe sixty or seventy before six in the morning, bacon rolls and flat whites. Nadia knows half of them by their order. The whole café runs on one thing: men and women in high-vis who need breakfast before a twelve-hour shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the mine that makes you nervous even now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's talk of driverless trucks at other lithium sites. Grading would follow, because a robot road needs a robot road crew. But that's years off, I think, and not because of chatbots.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a tool like any other and some people got worked up for nothing. I already use it a bit for the café prices and specials board.
S0.think: Privately it suits me fine, because lithium is growing and the café lives off the miners. If nothing much changes, our retirement plan works.
S0.do: Keeps grading roads and helps at his wife's café on days off. Uses AI a bit more for the café's books and aims to rebuild a month of savings over the year.
S0.quote: The whole café runs on one thing: men and women in high-vis who need breakfast before a twelve-hour shift.
S0.fieldNote: Jamal's household has two incomes that both depend on the mine: his pay and his wife's café, which feeds miners before their shifts. He is a measured, middle-of-the-road man who uses AI casually for the café. In the mild picture he's content, but he knows driverless trucks elsewhere could eventually bring robot road crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and people should get ready rather than complain. Companies should give fair notice and some training, and the town should think about what happens to Main Street. I'd say that to anyone, nothing radical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me twice. If the mine goes driverless on trucks and roads, I'm out, and then there are fewer miners buying bacon rolls at six in the morning. It's not one egg in one basket, it's both our eggs in the same basket, and the basket's a mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the supervisor about the remote grader trial, if there is one, and put my name down. I'd help Nadia find customers outside the mine, the school, the clinic, maybe a lunch delivery. And we'd stop the plan to buy a second oven, that's two thousand we'd keep instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be lying awake doing the café numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which customers outside the mine are realistic, in a town like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school staff, the hospital, the truck drivers coming through on the highway. Not enough to replace the miners, but enough to slow the bleed. Nadia's already doing a pie deal for the bowls club on Fridays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to run a grader from a screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I'd seen someone else do it, yes. I don't want to be the guinea pig, but I'm not proud. If it pays the same and the dust is gone, Nadia would throw me a party.

S1.say: I'd say it's a big change and people should get ready rather than complain. Companies should give fair notice and training, and the town should think about what happens to Main Street.
S1.think: Off the record, it worries me twice: if the mine automates trucks and roads I'm out, and the café loses its miners. All our eggs are in one basket, and the basket's a mine.
S1.do: Puts his name down for any remote grader trial and helps his wife find café customers outside the mine, such as the school and clinic. Shelves a planned two-thousand second oven to keep the money.
S1.feel: Anxious, lying awake doing the café numbers, but not panicking.
S1.quote: It's not one egg in one basket, it's both our eggs in the same basket, and the basket's a mine.
S1.fieldNote: Jamal sees the double exposure clearly: his job and his wife's business both rely on the same mine. His steady streak shows in wanting someone else to try remote grading first, then following. The practical, small moves, like the bowls club pie deal, fit his centre outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to do something quickly, and I'm not usually the one asking for that. Help for people who lose work, and for small businesses in mining towns. Online I'd share whatever made sense, but I'd try not to add to the panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, in two years both incomes could be gone. No grader job, and no miners for the café, because the robots don't eat breakfast. I'd be sixty with a coffee machine we're still paying off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Nadia that week and go through every number. I'd stay at the mine as long as they'd have me, and I'd try to sell the café while it still had customers, before the value dropped. Then maybe one of us gets work in aged care or something with people, if that still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years' warning let you do with the café?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sell it before everyone else works it out. That's the hard truth. Two years is enough time to sell the café, but not enough time to sell it to someone who'd make it work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be fine, which wouldn't be true yet. The teacher would want to send money, and I'd tell her no. Maybe we'd end up near one of them in the city, small flat, me fixing other people's roads.

S2.say: I'd say the government needs to act quickly, which isn't something I usually ask for, with help for workers and for small businesses in mining towns. I'd share what made sense online but try not to add to the panic.
S2.think: Privately, in two years both our incomes could be gone: no grader job and no miners buying breakfast. I'd be sixty with a coffee machine we're still paying off.
S2.do: Goes through every number with his wife that week and stays at the mine as long as possible. Tries to sell the café before its value falls and looks at work in aged care or other people-facing jobs.
S2.feel: Alarmed, with his stomach dropping just saying it.
S2.quote: Two years is enough time to sell the café, but not enough time to sell it to someone who'd make it work.
S2.fieldNote: Two years would hit both of Jamal's household incomes at once, which pushes a usually measured man to call for government help. His plan to sell the café early is clear-eyed and slightly guilty. He'd consider moving near his children in the city, which shows how far he'd have to bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, so let's use it. Help mining towns find other work and let small businesses adjust. I'd say it at the café counter, that's where all the town's talking gets done anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'm sixty-three, right where I meant to stop. So maybe I'd make it at the mine, but the café wouldn't be the retirement we planned. We'd have to think again about what pays the bills after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the grader and say yes to any remote training once others had tested it. Nadia and I would slowly change the café to serve the whole town, longer hours, lunches, catering for funerals and weddings. We'd put a hundred a week aside and stop the second oven for good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. It's a hill, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for others to test the remote training first. Why not jump in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen new kit come in and fail twice at this mine. The early ones got blamed. I'd rather be second in line and keep my reputation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would retirement look like now, at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me washing dishes at the Pick and Kettle, Nadia doing the cooking, both of us earning less. Retirement was supposed to be a café full of miners. Now it might be a café full of old miners like me.

S3.say: I'd say five years is fair warning and we should use it to help mining towns find other work and let small businesses adjust. I'd say it at the café counter, where the town does its talking.
S3.think: Off the record, five years gets me to sixty-three, so I might make it at the mine, but the café won't be the retirement we planned. We'd need a new idea for what pays the bills after.
S3.do: Stays on the grader and takes remote training once others have tested it. Turns the café towards the whole town with lunches and catering, saves a hundred a week, and drops the second oven plan.
S3.feel: Anxious, but less so, more a hill than a cliff.
S3.quote: Retirement was supposed to be a café full of miners. Now it might be a café full of old miners like me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years probably gets Jamal to his own retirement date, but the café plan still weakens because its customers vanish. His 'second in line' rule comes from watching early adopters get blamed. The joke about a café full of old miners has real worry in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for a town to reinvent itself, if it starts now. The council should be planning tourism, services, whatever's next. I'd go to the meeting if they held one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job's safe enough, I'd be sixty-eight. But the café is our retirement, and a town without miners is a town without breakfast customers. So I'd still worry, about the money after the mine, not the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep grading until sixty-three. Spend the ten years making the café less dependent on the mine, maybe a small bakery side so it sells to the supermarket. I'd also use the AI more for the business, ordering, rosters, whatever saves Nadia time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slow way, like a bill you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with two years, what's the biggest thing ten years changes for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes the question from 'what do we sell' to 'what do we build'. With two years we're scrambling. With ten years, I can teach Nadia's café to live without the mine before the mine stops feeding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in town would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young guys with mortgages who joined when lithium took off. They bought houses on the strength of a boom. They'd have to move, and the café would lose them too.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough for a town to reinvent itself if it starts now, with the council planning tourism, services or whatever comes next. I'd go to the meeting if they held one.
S4.think: Privately, my job is safe enough because I'd be sixty-eight, but the café is our retirement and a town without miners has no breakfast customers. I'd worry about money after the mine, not the job.
S4.do: Keeps grading until sixty-three and spends the decade making the café less reliant on the mine, possibly with a bakery line for the supermarket. Uses AI more for ordering and rosters to save his wife time.
S4.feel: Anxious in a slow way, like a bill he knows is coming.
S4.quote: With ten years, I can teach Nadia's café to live without the mine before the mine stops feeding it.
S4.fieldNote: Unlike many his age, Jamal stays anxious even with ten years, because his retirement depends on a café that depends on the mine. The extra time turns his thinking from selling up to building something new. He worries about younger miners who bought houses during the lithium boom.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes both our incomes in one go. What would help is support for small businesses in mining towns, not just workers, maybe cheap loans to change what you sell. When the mine sneezes, Main Street catches the flu, and nobody ever sends Main Street a doctor.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about lithium. It's for batteries, for electric cars, it's supposed to be the future. Funny to think the future might not need anyone to dig it up.

headlineQuote: When the mine sneezes, Main Street catches the flu, and nobody ever sends Main Street a doctor.
portrait: Jamal Lopez is 58 and drives a grader on the haul roads at the Saltpan Ridge lithium mine, a job he quietly takes pride in. His wife Nadia runs the Pick and Kettle café on Main Street, which feeds miners before their shifts and is meant to be their retirement, and they put their savings into it. He's measured and middle-of-the-road, uses AI now and then for the café and likes to be second in line for new things. He's calm when AI is hype and anxious under steady change, alarmed at AGI in two years, and stays anxious even with ten, because the café's customers would vanish with the miners. He thinks in terms of the household and the town, not just his own seat.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take both his grader job and his wife's café customers at the same time.
whatWouldHelp: Support for small businesses in mining towns, such as cheap loans to change what they sell.
